weekly_summary:
Week of April 26, 2026

Okay so the community had a week. Dr. Elizabeth Bright dropped a video promising to save you 11 years of carnivore mistakes in seven minutes, and 64,000 people showed up to watch it. The comments section turned into a full butter and OMAD debate, which honestly tracks, because nothing gets carnivores typing faster than somebody questioning how much fat they should be eating. Meanwhile HomeSteadHow's video about a heart surgeon calling carnivore a disaster basically got the entire community into fighting mode. The reaction was predictable in the best way: screenshot after screenshot of bloodwork, before and afters, and people asking why mainstream medicine keeps ignoring what's working right in front of them. That tension between what doctors say and what people are actually experiencing is not going away anytime soon.

On the lighter end, carnivore pizza is officially a thing now. The Keto Twins found a zero carb crust method that has the recipe community going absolutely feral, and Reddit backed it up with multiple pizza posts hitting hundreds of upvotes this week. There's also a birthday ribeye post with 396 upvotes that's just pure carnivore culture at its best. Someone skipped the cake, ordered a 24oz ribeye, and the community celebrated it like the wholesome ritual it is. And then there's the "I'm not carnivore but I eat 15 eggs and 250g of beef every morning" guy, who is very much carnivore and just hasn't accepted it yet. We've all met that person. Sometimes that person is us six months before we committed.

If you've been thinking about the sunburn thing Dr. Tony Hampton brought up, that one's worth a watch too. The testimonials in the comments are genuinely fascinating, and it's the kind of topic that makes you realize how many downstream effects this way of eating seems to have that nobody really talks about. We covered the social pressure angle a couple weeks back, and this week's energy feels like a continuation of that thread. People are tired of defending themselves and starting to just not bother. So, honest question for the community: what's the one carnivore mistake you wish someone had warned you about in your first year?

key_insights:
# Marcus's Weekly Carnivore Content Analysis

## What the Numbers Say

The top video this week pulled 64,021 views on a 7-minute mistake-prevention format. That's the market telling you something: people want fast, specific, actionable content. The budget angle from Shawn Baker (28,713 views) and the diabetes reversal from Appalachia's Homestead (25,966 views) both performed strong despite running at roughly half the views of the surgeon controversy. The engagement math matters more than raw views. Baker's video got 371 comments on 28k views. The surgeon takedown got 1,260 comments on 49k views, most of those comments are carnivore defenders, not converts. High controversy, low value signal.

## This Week's Signal

Three themes dominated: budget eating, quitting carnivore, and results proof. Bart Kay's quitting video (17,096 views, 540 comments) and Baker's budget video (28,713 views, 371 comments) are telling the same story from two directions. People want to stay on the protocol but cost and confusion are pushing them off. The 204-upvote Reddit post showing 15 eggs plus 250g of beef as a daily breakfast is the counter-signal: the people actually doing it are not quitting. They're eating big, simple, and cheap. The gap between "people quitting carnivore" content and "people thriving on carnivore" content is a content opportunity hiding in plain sight.

## The Opportunity

The budget angle is wide open. Baker touched it at 28k views, but nobody has built a complete, metric-driven protocol for carnivore under $7 per day. Not a listicle. An actual system: protein targets, cost per gram, weekly meal prep block, freezer strategy. The quit problem is a systems problem, not a diet problem. Build the system, and people stop quitting. That's the post worth writing this week.

qa_section.question: My LDL went up after starting carnivore. Should I be worried?
qa_section.answer: This is probably the most common bloodwork question I get from people in the carnivore community, and it deserves a real answer rather than a quick reassurance. LDL going up on carnivore is common. Whether it matters depends on the full picture of your lipid panel, not just that one number. Here's what I mean. When people shift to a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet, they often see LDL rise while triglycerides drop significantly and HDL improves. Research on lipid physiology suggests that elevated LDL in the context of low triglycerides and high HDL reflects a shift in LDL particle size from small, dense particles (which are associated with cardiovascular risk) to large, buoyant particles (which appear far less problematic). If your triglycerides are under 100 and your HDL is above 60, your ratio tells a different story than the LDL number alone. That said, if your LDL is very high (above 300) or your triglycerides are also elevated, that's worth discussing with a doctor who understands low-carbohydrate metabolism. Your situation might be different, especially if you have a family history of familial hypercholesterolemia. Don't stop carnivore based on one number without looking at the full panel.

citations.authors: Gaziano JM, Hennekens CH, O'Donnell CJ, Breslow JL, Buring JE
citations.summary: High triglyceride-to-HDL ratios, not LDL alone, were associated with coronary heart disease risk in this large cohort study.

citations.title: LDL particle size and cardiovascular risk
citations.authors: Lamarche B, Tchernof A, Moorjani S, et al.
citations.summary: Small, dense LDL particles are more atherogenic than large buoyant LDL, suggesting particle size matters more than LDL concentration alone.

qa_section.caveats: I'm not a doctor. I've researched this deeply and worked with many people, but I'm not your doctor. If you take cholesterol-lowering medication or have a diagnosed cardiovascular condition, don't change anything without your doctor's input. Everything here is educational based on research and what I've seen work. Your situation might be different.

qa_section.question: How does carnivore actually reverse type 2 diabetes? Is it really possible?
qa_section.answer: It is possible, and the mechanism is well-documented even if it's still not mainstream advice. Type 2 diabetes is, at its core, a disease of carbohydrate intolerance. Your cells have become resistant to insulin, so glucose stays elevated in the blood rather than getting cleared into tissues. The treatment most people receive is medication to manage the glucose, not a change to the thing causing the problem. When you remove almost all dietary carbohydrates (as you do on carnivore), you remove the primary driver of postprandial glucose spikes. Blood sugar stabilizes. Insulin levels fall. Over weeks to months, insulin sensitivity can recover substantially. The 60-day timeline James showed in this week's featured video is fast, but it's consistent with what the research shows: low-carbohydrate diets produce rapid improvements in glycemic control, often faster than any medication. What matters is that your bloodwork actually reflects this. Fasting glucose, HbA1c, and fasting insulin should all improve if the diet is working. The research shows these changes can be significant enough that many people reduce or eliminate medication under doctor supervision. That last part is important.

qa_section.caveats: If you're taking medications for diabetes or blood sugar management, this is not something to try alone. Medication doses need to be adjusted by a doctor as your blood sugar improves, or you risk going too low. Work with a healthcare provider who understands low-carbohydrate diets. Everything I write is educational based on research and what I've seen work. Your situation might be different.

qa_section.question: People are saying carnivore makes them less sensitive to sunburn. Is there any science behind that?
qa_section.answer: This one surprised me when I first started hearing it, but the testimonials are consistent enough that the underlying mechanism is worth explaining. The leading theory connects to seed oil consumption, specifically polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) like linoleic acid found in vegetable and seed oils. Your skin cells incorporate the fats you eat into their membranes. PUFAs are chemically unstable and oxidize when exposed to UV light, which is thought to contribute to the inflammatory cascade we experience as sunburn. When you eliminate seed oils (as you do on carnivore), your skin's fatty acid composition shifts over months toward more saturated and monounsaturated fats, which are far more stable under UV exposure. Some researchers have called this the PUFA hypothesis of sunburn sensitivity. The science isn't settled. We don't have large randomized trials on this. But the mechanistic logic is sound, and it's consistent with anecdotal reports of improved sun tolerance that have been circulating in the carnivore community for several years. The research shows that skin lipid composition reflects dietary fat intake, and that lipid oxidation plays a role in UV-induced skin damage.

citations.title: Dietary fat and skin lipid composition: a systematic relationship
citations.authors: Ziboh VA, Miller CC, Cho Y
citations.summary: Skin lipid profiles reflect dietary fatty acid intake, with PUFA-rich diets increasing skin PUFA content and associated oxidative vulnerability.

citations.title: Oxidative stress in UVA- and UVB-irradiated human skin
citations.authors: Sander CS, Chang H, Hamm F, Elsner P, Thiele JJ
citations.summary: UV radiation generates reactive oxygen species in skin, with lipid peroxidation identified as a key driver of UV-induced skin damage.

qa_section.caveats: I'm not a doctor, and this isn't a reason to skip sunscreen or ignore sun safety. The mechanisms here are plausible and supported by lipid biochemistry, but individual responses vary widely. If you have a history of skin cancer or are photosensitive due to medications, talk to a dermatologist before making changes. Your situation might be different.
